PREFACE AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
Pakistan had been described by many western and Indian
writers as a geographical nonsensity and a country disfigured at
birth. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, the well known Muslim
nationalist leader and the president of the All India Congress,
predicted that Pakistan, in its present shape, would not last more
than a-quarter of a century. His prediction came true. But not
because of the unique shape of the country, not even because of
the differences in language and culture of the two wings but
because of the follies of its people and because of the selfishness,
insincerity and short sightedness of its leaders. The most
important of all because of the ignominious role played by India 1
during the East Pakistan Crisis,
Come December each year, the nation is reminded of the
break-up of the country and the humiliation suffered by its armed
forces at the hands of its bitterest adversary. Unfortunately none
of the actors, dead or alive, who strutted about on the stage during
those crucial days, accepted that they faltered in advocating or
implementing the policies which led to the tragedy of the
disintegration of Pakistan.
The political leaders blame the army junta. The army generals '
blame the politicians, Independent political analysts blame both.
Indian writers harp on the tune of the exploitation of East Bengal
by the West Pakistani leadership. Pakistani authors highlight the
statements of a large number of influential Indians, including
Indira Gandhi, that the dismemberment of Pakistan would be in
India’s national interest and that India should not miss the
‘opportunity of a life time’ provided to them in 1971.
It is an irony of fate that the very people who were in the
)) Vanguard of the Pakistan movement, whose area was the only
Muslim majority province of undivided India which had a Muslim
League ministry and whose illustrious son had not only moved
but, allegedly, drafted the Lahore Resolution, fought a bitter
Struggle, thirty years later, to destroy a country which -they
themselves had helped to build.

How did this happen? what were the causes of the alienation of
the Bengalis from their co-citizens in the western wing? Why was
it not possible to stop the widening gap between the two halves of
Pakistan? Was the separate homeland for the Muslims of the
subcontinent merely a stepping stone for the Bengali politicians,
towards an independent Bangladesh? Could the armed forces have
avoided a humiliating surrender? These and many other related
' questions came to my mind during my research into the causes of
the tragic outcome.
This is the result of nearly three years of hard labour. It is
based on a deep study of documents, newspapers, articles, books
and personal interviews of those who were then at the helm of
affairs. The book focuses on the geo-strategic implication of a
country divided by a thousand miles of enemy territory. It brings
out the causes of the progressive alienation of the Bengalis from
West Pakistan. It highlights the political bitnglings of the civil and
military leadership during the first twenty-four years of Pakistan’s
existence. It analyses the war plans of India and Pakistan in 1971.
It focuses attention on the yole of India in this sordid drama and
finally it looks into the impact of the dismemberment of Pakistan
on India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. :
I have tried to disprove a few generalizations. The important
ones being that the dismantlement was a foregone conclusion
, because the only thing that was common between East and West
Pakistan was religion and the only link the PIA. The second ,
theory is the oft repeated accusation of the exploitation of East
Bengal by West Pakistan. I have tried to prove by facts and figures
that it is not entirely true. The third fallacy which does not stand
scrutiny is a fact often quoted by Indian academicians that there
was a deliberate attempt by the Punjabi hierarchy to keep the
East Pakistani’s out of the civil service and the armed forces. It is
true that the Bengalis did not have a share in the government in
~ proportion to their population but the causes lay elsewhere.

In 1974, the late Lieutenant General Agha Ibrahim Akram,
well known author of the book, Sword of Allah, told me about
writing his second book on the advent of Islam in Iran. On my
saying "why do you not write about the dismemberment of
Pakistan?" he replied "I do not write about defeat". I too felt the
same way, when it was suggested to me that I should write about
the Indo-Pakistan War of December, 1971, particularly because it
would mean treading on the toes of many of my senior colleagues —~
with whom I had developed a close friendship after retirement.
But then I recalled Brigadier S. K. Dalvi’s book the ‘Himalayan
Blunder’ where he had candidly criticized his own authorities for
the mistakes made during the Sino-Indian Conflict of 1962 in
which the Indian Army was humbled. The Indian leaders
benefitted by the criticism.
I picked up courage to try and analyse the events that led to
the break-up of Pakistan with no axe to grind. The dust-en-gulfed
NDC thesis was taken out of the shelf and re-read.
I was fully aware of the enormous difficulties 1 would face in
reaching the truth. President Agha Muhammad Yahya Khan,
Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman, Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto, General Abdul
Hamid Khan and Admiral 8. M. Ahsan had all passed away,
taking with them many facts, the disclosures of which would have
helped in unfolding the truth further.
Researchers and historians have to fall back on the written
word when they wish to carry forward their learned profession.
Nations must learn from past mistakes. Younger generations
must not repeat the errors of their elders. It is in this spirit that I
have chosen to carry out an independent analysis of the reasons
for the break up of the country. Nearly all those directly or
indirectly involved in the decision making process in the critical
years between 1968-1971 have been interviewed. Some several
times over and for extended periods of time.
__ After a lapse of twenty three years a lot of facts have come to
light but not all have been published. Most of the writers are from
across the border. Not many Pakistani authors have attempted to
recall bitter memories. Pakistan’s case has gone by default. It is
hoped that this book would encourage, other writers, specially

Background
Geographical Characteristics
East Pakistan, lying at the eastern extremity of the Indian
subcontinent, differed from its western wing in its geographic
location, physical features, socio-economic conditions and in its
security environment. Separated from the rest of Pakistan by
1,600 kilometres of Indian territory it was more easily vulnerable
to internal and external pressures than the rest of the country.
Abul Kalam Azad opined that Mr. Jinnah did not seem to realize
that geography was against him!. He was not too far wrong.
With an area covering 143,998 square kilometres it was
smaller in size than almost all other provinces of Pakistan. Its
population of 40 million in 1947 was, however, greater than all the
four administrative units in the west combined. This numerical
superiority coupled with the volatile nature of an ever increasingly
frustrated community shifted the dynamics of power to the streets
of East Bengal. .
East Pakistan, except for a very small border with Burma, was
surrounded on all sides by India. In the west lay the Indian state
of West Bengal. In the north was Magalaya and Assam, in the east
Tripura and Mizogram and in the south the Indian dominated Bay
of Bengal. Geography, therefore, very much favored India if and
when it decided to use its military instrument to achieve its
political objective. Pakistan’s eastern wing could easily be cut off
from the other half, in fact from the rest of the world, by India
because of its peculiar geographic location.
The three main river systems, each broad enough to look like a
sea of water, divided the country into four isolated regions. The
western sector lay between the Bay of Bengal and the
Ganges/Padma with Khulna, Jessore and Faridpur being the
main towns. The northern portion was wedged in between the
Jamuna and the Brahmaputra/Meghna. Saidpur and Rangpur in
the north and Bogra further south were the nodal points. East
and south of the Meghna lay the tea gardens of Sylhet and the
- undulating ground around Comilla and Chittagong.

Tragedy of Errors
Strategic Implications
These formidable water obstacles, unbridged except in very
few places, alongwith a maze of interconnecting water channels
split the defenders into isolated pockets and gave advancing
enemy columns secure flanks. They presented no obstacle when
moving along them but were almost insurmountable to those who
dared to cross over them against opposition.
The 6,000 square kilometres Deltaic region, along the coast
with its numerous creeks and water inlets, with its swamps and
thickets, was impregnable to friends and foes alike. The forests of
the Sunderbans, along the southwest coast, immortalized by the
famous English novelist, John Masters, and those of Mahdopur
near Dacca restricted movement in those areas. The Chittagong
Hill Tracts, in the east rising to heights of 2,000 feet, forested and
mountainous, was ideal for guerrilla actions.
Mention must be made of the area around Dacca, known in
military circles as the Dacca bowl or the Dacca triangle. A flat and
open country about a 100 kilometres wide and 60 kilometres deep.
It lay between three major river systems with the mighty Jamuna
and Ganges in the west, the Dareshwari river in the south and the
Meghna in the east. The only approach to Dacca which did not
need the crossing of a major river was from the north,
Communications .
Communication infrastructure was poor. Roads were narrow,
and few and far between. Most of them frequently ended on river
banks from where the loads had to be transferred on to steamers
and back again on to the single lane asphalt highway. Chittagong
and Khulna were two sea-going ports with Chandpur providing
only an inland water transport (IWT) facility. A railway line did
connect the capital to Rajshahi in the west, Saidpur in the north,
Sylhet in the north-east and the port of Chittagong in the south,
but not without the restriction of unloading and loading on to
ferries as construction of railway bridges across the rivers was
only possible in one or two places. Most of the movement, both
civilian and military, was along rivers and streams by naukas
(country boats) and steamers. With cross country movement
difficult, even during the dry season, all major traffic had to be
confined to the few available metalled roads, interdiction of which
became comparatively easier during war.

Geographical Characteristics
Although the communication network in East Pakistan was
generally poor the roads and railways leading to the international /
border from Indian West Bengal were well] developed. Calcutta, “
the largest city of India and the headquarters of India’s Eastern
Command, was only 100 kilometres away from the Pakistani town
of Jessore. It was connected to it by several metalled roads and
broadguage railway tracks. Assembly of forces on the Indian side
was easier.
Vulnerable Salients .
The geographical configuration of East Pakistan created a
number of salients and narrow necks of land which, while making
them vulnerable to attacks, also provided opportunities to disrupt
India’s vital lines of communication. Patchagarh salient in the
north-west jutted into the Siliguri gap connecting West Bengal
with Assam. Even a small thrust northwards could create
difficulties for India’s Eastern Command. Though 40 kilometres
long it had a width of only 10 kilometres. A major road from
Jalpaiguri (India) to Tatulia ran through it. Kurigram salient a
little further east had only a width of 6 kilometres. Belonia east of
Comilla was surrounded on three sides by India and posed a
serious problem for the defenders. The most vulnerable neck of
land in East Pakistan was Feni which was only a stone’s throw
away from India. An advance of only a few kilometres ‘could severe
Chittagong port and a large tract of East Pakistan, without any
major effort, from the rest of the province.
Climate
East Bengal, lying astride the tropic of cancer, had a hot and
humid climate. Temperatures in summer rose up to 33 C°
(91 °F). Not very hot from South Asian standards but what made
the living uncomfortable was the humidity. Bengal catches the full
blast of the south-west monsoons. With an average rainfall of over
2,500 millimeters (100 inches), concentrated during the period
between April and September, major military operations could
take place during the winter months only.
Demography
The Bengalis came from a different racial stock than their co-
citizens in the north and north-west of India. While the latter felt
proud that through their viens flowed the blood of the Aryans

from Central Asia the Bengalis were quite content pty ene
the original inhabitants of East Bengal.. Althoug Bengal t :
Persians, Turks and Mughals also ventured as far be ce " » the
500 years of Muslim rule injected only the Muslim ~ eee
not change their physical characteristics. Unlike ine fete Ss and
the Pathans the Bengalis were relatively Bnei arker and
thinly built. The difference in physical features gave the
northerners a false sense of racial superiority which was reflecteg
in their attitude and social behavior towards their brethren in the
east. About 87 percent of the population of East Bengal were
Muslims. Around 10 percent were Hindus and the remaining 3
percent was shared between Budhists and Christians.
The Muslims in the eastern wing, unlike the West Pakistanis,
, were not split into castes and sub castes, and were more
» | homogeneous than the rest of their countrymen. They could,
therefore, put up a more united resentment against statements
and policies which they perceived to be damaging to their self
esteem and interest.
There is no doubt that the Bengali Muslims, who constituted
57% of the population in undivided Bengal, were greatly
influenced by the Hindus who had achieved a position of
dominance under the British rule. This was so because after the
unsuccessful war of independence, known generally as the Great
Indian Mutiny (1857), the British distrusted the Muslims of
Bengal. Sir W. W. Hunter, a British civil servant, writing in 1887,
noted that the Bengali Mussulman was thoroughly dejected and
frustrated as "every honourable walk of life was closed to him and
that he was excluded from the share of power and of the
emoluments of government which he hitherto almost monopolized
and saw them passed into the hands of the hated Hindus".
During the 190 years of British rule the Hindus dominated the -
Bengali landscape. Lands, business, education, government |
service all were in their hands. Major General Khalil-ur-Rahman, |
a Bengali officer from Khulna, recalls the environment in.his city |
during his school days. He remembers the Hindu festivals of
Durga Puja, Holi and Devalj being celebrated on the streets. The |
birthday of the Holy Prophet {Peace Be Upon Him) and other
tl one festivals were confined to within the walls of the

25
Geographical Characteristics
Islamic subjects were not taught in the schools at Khulna on
the contrary the curricula included aspects of the Hindu faith.
Islamic education, became the responsibility of the parents and
not of the teachers, who in any case where mostly Hindus*®. The
term Bengali meant a Hindu Bengali. Muslim Bengalis were
simply known as Muslims. "Though not actually social outcasts
they were not allowed into Hindu homes even after independence"
said General Khalil. Slowly, however, this treatment had its
negative impact and the Muslims of Bengal began to resent the
overlordship of their Hindu neighbours - which eventually led to
their demand for a separate homeland along with the rest of the
Muslims of India.
_ Historical Perspective
Bengal was conquered by the Mughals in 1202 AD by
Muhammad Bakhtyar Khilji, a subordinate commander of Sultan ,
Qutubuddin Aiybak‘*. It was the first province of the Mughal (
Empire to pass fully into the hands of the British. Since the
British had snatched power from the Muslims they were
apprehensive of any attempt by them to try and regain their lost
kingdom. They, therefore, made a concerted plan to suppress the
‘Muslims and encourage the Hindus in their newly acquired
domain of Bengal.
Partition of Bengal and its Annulment
The dominance of the Hindu landlord, businessmen and
traders increased to such an extent in Bengal that the Muslims
demanded the partition of the province so that they could free
themselves from the Hindu Bhadrulok (landlord). Bengal was
partitioned in 1905. and the districts of Dacca, Rajshahi and
Chittagong (later to become part of Pakistan) were separated from
Western Bengal. "The Hindus considered the partition of Bengal
as an attempt to create a Muslim state in Eastern Bengal"®. Most

Causes of Alienation
The most significant effect of the geographical separation of the
two wings of Pakistan was the alienation of East Bengal from the
rest of the country. Many were the reasons put forward by the
_ Bengalis for_the bitterness they felt towards their co-citizens in
the west. Some were, of course, exaggerated to achieve the
objective of selfish individuals. A few were completely false and
part of a disinformation campaign. But none of the issues were so
great, in the beginning, to be unsurmountable.
What was needed was a clearer understanding of the unique ;
nature of Pakistan’s geography and its peculiar demographic ~~
characteristics. A sincere effort was also required, not only to
devise, but to implement, policies which could have removed the ~
suspicion and mistrust which had crept into the minds of the
people on both sides. The politicians, military leadership, \
bureaucrats and businessmen all shared this responsibility. «
Tragically they failed to deliver. Mistakes were made soon after
independence. Regional _ political leadeys and frustrated
intellectuals capitalised on them. Errors kept multiplying;
emotions kept rising; demands and their suppression kept
growing till it was too late to prevent the dismemberment of the
country aided and abetted by a hostile neighbour.
/
What were the main causes for the glienation? These could be
grouped under cultural, economic, political and military. Behind
some of them was a foreign hand initially hidden and towards the
final phase brazenly open.
Language Issue
A major factor which alienated the Bengalis from the rest of
the Pakistanis was the language issue. National authorities failed
to understand the deep attachment the Bengalis had for their
mother tongue.

No where, in Pakistan, was this more apparent than in its

Their dress, diet and social customs differed from the rest. Their
love for dance, music and poetry brought them closer to the
Bengali Hindus. It is also true that the Hindu elite had dominated
the social and economic life of Bengal and there was much greater
fusion between theitwo religious communities in that province. So
be it!
In India the West Bengalis are very different to the East
Punjabis and more so because they belong to different faiths.
Their religion, outward appearance, dress and dietary habits are
not the same. the Madrasis differ considerably from the Hindus of
the United Provinces in race, colour, language, customs but yet
they are all Indians. Why then should such differences have
become a cause for the separation of the two wings of Pakistan?
None of the demographic dissimilarities would have altered the
loyalty of the Bengalis towards Pakistan if they had not been
) treated as inferiors.or if they had not been deprived of their
legitimate rights.
The language riots had already resulted in a bitter feeling
against the Centre. Emotions were again aroused when Governor

but from the urban elite, banned the songs of Rabinder Nath

The most vociferous complaint by the intellectuals and the
politicians of East Pakistan was the so-called economic domination

pains to highlight the imbalance in the trade between the two
wings, the transfer of capital from the East to the West, the
increasing gap in the per capita income and the slow rate of
economic growth in East Pakistan. .
G.W. Choudhry, a senior Bengali civil servant, who was
associated with decision making at various levels, considered
economic disparity as the "most serious challenge to the unity of |
Pakistan". According to him “East Pakistanis felt that their |
interests were not safe with West Pakistan controlling the
economic resources"®’, Self interested political leaders made full
use of the figures quoted by them to bring out the dire need of

Most of the statistics mentioned were indeed correct. However,
differences in the standard of living, and a gap in industrial
development did exist even before Independence between the
provinces of Punjab and East Bengal. It continued to remain and
even widen during the twenty four years of a United Pakistan. It
_ Still exists even after two decades of the emergence of Bangladesh.
The question that needs answering is as to why that was so?
Was it a deliberate act of the central leadership to deprive East
« Pakistan of its due share of economic development? Was it due to

the utopia of a homogeneous development throughout their
countries?

The facts mentioned in the earlier chapter certainly give the
impression to a casual reader that East Pakistan was

According to Mahboobul Haq, “underdeveloped countries do

quick returns are expected. Gustav Papanek maintains that

inequality”. ”

not half as prosperous as Washington and New York. The North-
west territories of Canada have a lower standard of living than
Ontario and Quebec in the Ae Financial resources in a free

quicker and greater returns. =.

The Basic Principles Report of 1950 which was the first
attempt made at formulating a constitution for the country
recommended a parliamentary system of government with a
bicameral legislature. The lower house was to comprise of
representatives from both the wings based on the basis of
population. This would have ensured a larger number of members
from East Bengal. In the upper house equal representation was to
be given to all the federating units irrespective of their size, This is
the practice taken from the mother of parliaments. So is the case
in the Rajya Sabha in India where each state has been allotted
equal number of seats. Uttar Pradesh, with the largest population
has the same representation in the Rajya Sabha as Rajastan with
a very small population.
In the first constituent assembly out of a total of 74 members”
44 were Bengalis. Again in 1954, the new constituent assembly ,
accorded a greater number of seats to East Bengal. There were 44”
members from the eastern wing out of a total of 79 seats!. This
should have more than satisfied the demand of the East Bengalis.
As regards the two most important. posts of the governor-
general and the prime minister of the country, after the death of
the founder of the nation and that of Liaqat Ali Khan, both the |
appointments were held by Bengalis. Khwaja Nazimuddin ~
followed the Quaid-e-Azam, as the head of state and Muhammad ;
Ali Bogra became the chief executive after Liagat Ali Khan. If
Nazimuddin was not considered to be a blue-blooded Bengali
because he came from the Urdu speaking family of the Nawabs of
Dacca, West Pakistanis should hardly be blamed. The fact that.he
eventually proved to be weak and indecisive, though thoroughly
. honest and sincere, was again not a deliberate attempt to keep the
Bengalis down. In 1948 there was no other Bengali leader who
could be elevated to the highest post in the land. Both Maulvi _,
Fazlul Haq and Hussein Shaheed Suharwardy stood discrete VA
because of their dilly dallying on the ideas of a United Bengal.
Other Bengali politicians had still not come on the centre stage.
Suharwardy did, however, become the prime minister of Pakistan
In the late fifties.

On January 29, 1968 Field Marshal Ayub suffered a severe

constitution the speaker of the national assembly should have

was not done as Ayub never trusted him. This deliberate violation

the president went to England for a medical check up. He once
again departed from the democratic practice by keeping Mr. Abdul
Jabbar Khan away from the presidential chair. This encouraged
his opponents to increase the pressure on him to quit his office.

and the men in the street joined him in his tirade against the

provinces shall be so united in a federation that the independence,
territorial integrity and: the national solidarity of Pakistan are

But at no time was Mujib warned of violating the LFO. In fact
the President did not consider anything wrong with the 6 Points.

was not against Martial law Regulation 60°25, Perhaps General
Yahya and his close aides felt that the 6-Points formula was
merely an election slogan to win votes and that the Awami League
would modify them when it comes to framing the constitution.
The reality of the situation during the electioneering campaign
in 1970 was that Mujib-ur-Rahman, the rabble rouser_that he
was, had succeeded in galvanising the vast majority of the
Bengalis towards attaining their goal of maximum autonomy
bordering on separation. Unfortunately no government at the
Centre, military or civil, could have prevented Mujib and his
followers from preaching his 6 Points which by then had become
the demand of the vast majority of the Bengalis.
Although Yahya kept repeating that he would not tolerate.a?y
scheme which would mean the break up of the country he had n°
| power left to enforce his statements. His military commanders in
[, Hast Pakistan were not inclined nor had they the military muscle
‘jo face the people of East Pakistan in 1970.

The election campaign, which ran for over ei
was the longest in the history of the mileautonne Pareto’
a year politicians were given a free hand to whip up emotions
against their rivals and in the case of East Pakistan against the
Contte and the so-called Punjabi exploitation of East Bengal.
_-'Twenty four political parties participated in the elections. Most
of them with little or no public support. None were national in -
character. Almost all were regional in their outlook. The Awami
League did put up four of its candidates in West Pakistan but
none succeeded to get a seat in the national assembly. Bhutto’s
People’s Party did not even attempt to challenge the Awami
League in East Pakistan. The elections were, therefore, totally
regional in its context. Out of the four major political parties, the
Awami league was drumming up its anti-West propaganda and
arousing the Bengalis to rise up for their demand of maximum
regional autonomy which could have been interpreted as a veiled
cry_for total independence. To avoid being dubbed as a purely
regional political party the Awami League did show a token
_ presence in West Pakistan. The fig leaf, however, could not hide
its actual contours.

out of jail several times for opposing the policies of the rulers
\ began his political career before Partition as a member of the
Muslim League. He took an active part in the Pakistan movement
but remained a nationalist at heart. But he too had second
thoughts. "The Lahore Resolution did mention two states"*® said
Khondkar to the author when being interviewed at his modest
second storey flat in a down town residential area of Dhaka.
He dilated quite a while on the question of regional autonomy,
summing it up by saying "after you got the cake you wanted it all y

the domineering attitude of the West Pakistani leeatorett was

should be here (in, Bangladesh). "History justifies it, numbers

There were, of course, many politicians in East Pakistan who
were against Mujib and his 6-Points formula. Nur-ul-Amin and
Mahmood Ali continued to address meetings also and drew
reasonable crowds. They criticised secularism, socialism and
communism. The intelligence agencies were wrongly impressed
by the size of the audience at such meetings and gave the
impression to their higher authorities that there was a gradual
assertion of rightist forces in East Pakistan, which was not true,
The so-called alliance of Islam-pasand parties was being wrongly
interpreted in intelligence circles as a "useful development”.
Fazlul Quader Choudhry of the Pakistan Muslim League
(Quader Group) was also critical of the Awami League’s demand
for full regional autonomy and was against slogans of ‘Joy
Bangla’. But his voice did not carry very far and got lost in the
thunder of pro-Awami League demonstrators at his meetings. So
did the voice of Ata-ur-Rahman of the National Pakistan League
who criticised Mujib for his dictatorial role.
The Awami League, which even before the election campaign
had begun to show its muscle, became a fascist. and militant
organisation which was not prepared to brook any rival. It was
determined to crush by force any opposition to its formula for total
regional autonomy. Consequently no other political party was ~
allowed to hold public meetings in East Pakistan. The Jamaat-e-
Islami (JI) meeting being held at Paltan Maidan, Dacca, on
January 18, 1970 was disturbed and not allowed to continue. Four
days later its offices were raided and all its literature destroyed.
Similarly the meetings of the Pakistan Democratic Party were
disrupted on February 1, 1970 and two of its newspapers the
Bunyad and Sangram were gutted‘! by the Awami League
workers,

After the Elections
In countries where democracy has taken root and democratic
traditions have been well established the frenzy and emotional
outbursts by opposing candidates subside after the elections.
Every one gets back to business as usual The defeated politician
does not wait a second longer to congratulate the winner as soon
as it becomes certain that he has secured the majority vote. On
the date specified the newly elected head of government or head of
state 1s sworn in with all the fan fare and jubilation reserved for
such occasions. The outgoing chief leaves the office with grace to
pursue his academic activities.
Unfortunately in most developing States the fight goes on even
after the election results have been announced. The results are a
challenged. Statements are made by both the winning and losing
candidates which heighten tension. Victory celebrations taunting
the losers are arranged. Attempts are made to disrupt the transfer
of power by the newly elected loyal opposition. Frustrated
politicians threaten to use street power to negate the verdict of the
people. Fears are expressed that the victorious party will act
against the interest of the state. Such was the state of affairs after
the December, 1970 elections,

mistake on this point" said the General!3®, But it is not military

Unfortunately democracy and democratic traditions had not

unconstitutional role of administering the country.
In 1969, Field Marshal Ayub had become extremely unpopular,
his health was failing. A bunch of self interested politicians were
quarrelling with each other on the Pakistani stage with the men
in uniform waiting in the wings. What should Ayub have done in
such a situation. After 10 years of martial law and a decade of
controlled democracy the people were agitating not only against
an individual but against a political system which had been thrust

affected by tumultuous events in their country, more sis if ethnic
issues are involved. So it was with the Bengali elements in the
military establishment, particularly those serving in Kast Pakistan
during the days when the election campaign was in full swing.
Although the Awami League was not demanding separation from
West Pakistan initially, Sheikh Mujib-ur-Rahman and his
lieutenants were leaving no stone unturned to widen the existing
gulf between the two wings. He was, without any restraint,
playing to the tune of Bengali nationalism. His fiery speech on
March 7, at the race course grounds, Dacca, left no doubt that he
had finally given the call for an independent Bangladesh although
he did not declare it openly.

This practice was followed by the Indian and Pakistan army

East Bengal Regiments (EBR)
The first and second battalions of the East Bengal Regiment
were raised in Kurmitola (Dacca) in 1948 when General Ayub
Khan was the GOC in East Bengal. Their class composition was
100 percent Bengali. General Ayub did not raise any objection to
this change in the composition of the East Bengal Regiment units.
perhaps due to the fact that initially it was presumed that they
would only serve in the eastern wing. The question of a whole unit
revolting could never have crossed his mind a year after the
creation of Pakistan. A five percent quota for recruitment of
Bengali personnel had, however, been placed which later was
removed and so by 1965/66 five battalions of the East Bengal
Regiment were on the ground.
As more and more EBR units were raised and some began
serving in West Pakistan also, problems arising out of linguistic
and cultural differences began to raise their head. Lieutenant

Jessore. Each sector was composed of six wings of 450 men each.
Most of the men were Bengalis while their officers came both

wing.

with frustration when he was not promoted to the rank of a
brigadier and was moved over to a less sensitive post. He became

given him a fair deal. Osmany was the right man to organise a

Tactics
Initially, between March and April, the Mukti Bahini was used
to support the Indian Border Security Forces in keeping the
.. Pakistan army away from the international frontier to enable the
Indian army to gain as much information about the trans-border
terrain as possible.
j In the second phase, from May to July, the Muktis dressed in
civilian clothes were required to penetrate deep inside their own
country and carry out subversive activities. Blowing up of bridges,
blocking roads, ambushing convoys and assassinating isolated
army personnel. (700 trained guerrillas were inducted into
Faridpur district alone by the middle of May)®5, The so-called
miscreants, undistinguishable from the rest, were everywhere in
East Pakistan, present even in government offices. By day they
/were ordinary citizens by night they were guerrillas. An Indian’
writer accepts that many of them were Hindus wearing dhotis
(lion cloth around the waist worn by Hindus)??. Workers
instigated by the Muktis, damaged 38 Jute mills in Khulna and
Mymensingh”*. In the battle of Feni (June 1971) the Mukti Bahini
claimed to have killed 500. A.K. Kamaraz-Zaman reported to his
Indian mentor that 13,000 Pakistani soldiers have been killed
between March 25 and June 12, 197179. Mukti Bahini supported
by regular Indian troops attacked and captured Bariab Bazaar on
the Indo-East Pakistan border on June 20, 1971. A commando
element of two companies led by Lieutenant Colonel Shakurjan
had to be dropped by helicopters across the river to recapture the
area. In this action the Mukti Bahini suffered 500 casualties.
Shakurjan lost one of his men.
} In the third Phase which began in August, 1971 the Mukti
Bahini, supported by Indian artillery fire from across the border,
were directed to attack Pakistani border posts and ‘liberate’
vulnerable enclaves which could later be used as jumping off
points by the Indian army.
A need was felt to provide some political guidance to the so-
called freedom fighters. The Indian government, therefore, formed
a political committee of eight activists on September 9, from
members of the self-styled Bangladesh goverment in exile, to
ensure a greater control over the Mukti Bahini®.

The Mukti Bahini were not al] trained to fight side by side with
the Indians. In fact they were never considered to be a force which
could withstand a concerted battle. They were Mostly trained for
insurgency operations and to work behind enemy lines to cut off
their routes of withdrawal. Though some were trained for regular
warfare as well.
The Mukti Bahini were not as effective as it was expected as
they had not been able to absorb the training imparted to them in
the few months between April and November. There were a large
number of civilians who had been recruited into the Mukti Bahini
who needed more time, to handle mortars and to direct artillery
fire accurately. The command and control element was also not
upto the standard of a well trained fighting force. Since they had
no operational experience they would not have been able to evict a

The primary task of the army is to defend a country’s
international borders against any external threat. A subsidiary
role, which = certain circumstances assumes considerable
significance, is to act in aid of civil power to quell an insurgency
against the state, or simply to maintain law and order. Towards

prepared, updated and kept ready.
In normal peace time conditions, when calm and harmony

administrative files in the adjutant general’s branch of any army
headquarters. But when the country is faced with internal
disturbances and the writ of the government-in-power begins to
be seriously challenged military commanders with foresight begin

cities was fast returning to normal. No indepth study of the mood
of the people of East Pakistan after the military action, was made
by the intelligence agencies. No investigative réporting was
carried out.
Military action was launched to restore the authority of the
government and save the country from total disintegration. This
action was mostly directed at the elimination of the rebellious
elements of the East Bengal Regiment and the East Pakistan
Rifles and other 2nd-Line Forces including the civil police, It was

When an offer of ceasefire was made by Pakistan’s Eastern
Command, Kissinger called General N. A. M. Raza, who had by
then replaced Mr. Agha Hilaly as the ambassador of Pakistan in
Washington, and asked him not to give an unconditional ceasefire

Jack Anderson’s contention that a superpower confrontation
could have taken place in the Bay of Bengal because of Nixon’s tilt
towards Pakistan, only betrays his personal animosity against
Nixon and his pro-Indian stance. Neither the Soviet Union nor the
United State’s vital interests were at stake in East Pakistan. Nor
were the assembly of forces and the dispositions during the Indo-
Pakistan war such,that a conflict between the two superpowers
could have taken place. When the US naval flotilla crossed the
straits of Malacca a ceasefire was already being negotiated. It was
only a question of time when the obvious results would be known.
A nuclear holocaust at this stage, as envisaged by Anderson, was
,ho where on the cards. It is a pity that internationally known
columnists cannot tear themselves away from personal rivalries
and pre-conceived ideas.
After the war was over , William Rogers, who had been
opposing Nixon’s so-called tilt towards Pakistan, did realise that
the use of force to solve a political problem in the neighbourhood
was not justified. He is reported to have said on January 5, 1972
If every political problem that is created in the world justifies the
use of force then there is no end to war'29, |

The Muslim Ummah
In spite of the expectations of a certain segment of the society
in Pakistan, none of the Muslim countries gave any substantial
support to Pakistan in its hour of need. The internal situation had
deteriorated to such an extent that even believers of the same God
did not feel it prudent to burn their fingers in the flames which
were engulfing East Pakistan.
A country should only expect support from its friends if either,
their national interest is at stake, or the aggressor is a common
enemy. In both cases internal harmony and cohesion within the
_ country remains the bottom line.

The geographical separation of the two wings of Pakistan made
it virtually impossible to plan for a co-ordinated defence of the
whole of the country. The options available were either to raise
two self-contained independent armed forces, each capable of
defending its own area of responsibility against a numerically
superior enemy, or to provide for a minimum force in a less
vulnerable region with the major defensive strength lying in the
other. |

dismembering Pakistan. Economically, however, such an option
could not have been sustained and the danger of the country

basic necessities would have been very much there.
In the latter case one or the other wing would remain

Too Little Too Late
The scene in East Pakistan had changed completely after the
military action in March, 1971. The Bengali units had deserteq
and had gone over to India, the civilians, though subdued ang
frightened because of the fear of the stick, had turned againgt the
Pakistan armed forces.
In view of the growing threat from India in support of the
Mukti Bahini and the need to control an ever increasing hostile
population more troops were flown in to East Pakistan soon after
the military action. Elements of 9 Infantry Division and 16
Infantry Division began arriving by air via Sri Lanka. The two
newly inducted divisions came without their guns and armour,
They could only carry their infantry weapons and even lacked
engineer support. The Corps signal battalion was only sanctioned
in March, 1971.
Lieutenant General Amir Abdullah Khan Niazi (54) took over
the command of the eastern theatre of operations from General
Tikka Khan on 7 April. He was a highly decorated officer having
earned a Military Cross and Mention in Despatches as a junior
officer during World War II and a Hilal-e-Jurat in the Indo-
Pakistan War of 1965. As an officer in 8 Punjab Regiment he had
seen active service in Egypt, Iraq, Palestine, Burma, Malaysia,
Singapore and Java and hence fighting in different environment
was not new to him. But what affected his professional ability in
East Pakistan was his rigid ideas and his false sense of pride of not
falling back in the face of the enemy. His Mianwali background,
and his limited academic achievements may have had much to do
with his narrow military outlook.
General Niazi had earned good confidential reports in his
career but his superiors had emphasised his knowledge and flair
for tactics only. Command of an independent theatre requiring *
understanding of national Strategy was not what he had been Oe
out to be. He was a Shera (lion) but only at the lower net
command. He was "practical and bold" but unable or owing ‘
visualise the intentions and capabilities of a powerful part
General Yahya, however, could not find any other senior ° few of
go to East Pakistan in April, 1971. It is believed that quite @
them got out of it when asked to do so.

By the time Niazi came on the scene the Pakistan army had re-
' established the writ of the central government in most of the
province. The troops, along with the civil armed forces, (by now
manned purely by the West Pakistanis) were manning most of the
outposts along the international border. By the middle of May,
1971 all appeared quiet on the Eastern front.
This lull before the impending storm had created a false sense
of security. Niazi, based his operational plan for the defence of
East Pakistan more on bravado than on a cool assessment of the
military situation. Operational Instructions Number 3 of 15 July,
1971 contemplated a forward posture with strong points and
fortresses which were made logistically self sufficient to fight a
battle lasting for atleast thirty days if by-passed. Twenty five
fortresses and nine strong points were designated. All, however,
could not be adequately manned due to shortage of troops. Dacca
was the nerve centre, but no troops were left to defend it.
A fresh plan for the defence of East Pakistan, was sent in
August, 1971, to GHQ by Eastern Command. In addition to the
development of major towns as fortresses and strong points with a
firm commitment to defend Dacca at all costs. The plan included
offensive actions against Tripura in the east. Siliguri in the north,
Krishannagar in the West. The plan was duly approved by GHQ
which went even further and directed Eastern Command to plan
on posing a threat to Calcutta and the capture of Farrakha
barrage. Targets for the Special Service Groups in Indian territory
Were to be selected. |
It is normal for a defender to plan local offensive actions to
improve their defensive position and deny launching pads for the
*nemy immediately in front of their defended areas. But major
offensive operations much beyond the range of own guns and
Without air support when troops are insufficient to fulfil their
primary task is sheer folly. One can only feel frustrated on the |
lack of realism on the part of the military leadership at GHQ at |
that time, With the rear areas insecure and the home base
“ompletely cut off; the air force and the navy particularly non-
€xistent in East Pakistan; with the third dimension totally absent,
‘0 have thought of making such ambitious plans could only come
from highly inflated egos. |

The actual deployment saw companies spread thinly along the
border with battalions holding frontages as much as 30 miles in
some sectors (Military manuals recommend a 1 mile frontage for a
battalion with a depth of half a mile or so). Extended frontages,
lack of depth in defence, forward posture, no reserves at division
and command level were the major weaknesses of the defensive
plan before the start of hostilities. The plan of falling back after
the battle was joined was also unsound particularly when the rear
areas were not only unsafe but it was a question of having an
enemy all around.
PAF could only spare one squadron of 12 F86Fs for East
Pakistan. Air commodore Inam-ul-Haq who was the Air Officer
Commanding (AOC) in Dacca had only two airfields Tejgaon and
Kurmitola (both around Dacca) to operate from.
Rear Admiral Muhammad Sharif, Flag Officer Commanding
Kast Pakistan, had no naval ships to guard the ports of Chittagong
and Chalna. A few gunboats was his entire navy in East Pakistan.

Concept of Operation
General Aurora decided to carry out multi-directional thrusts
while keeping Dacca as the main objective. His operational policy
was:
a. Avoiding frontal attacks
b. By-passing strong points
c. Para drops to speed up operations
d. Infiltration by Mukti Bahini and rebels to cause dislocation
in rear areas
e. Preventing Pakistani troops from falling back into the
Dacca bowl and
f. Reaching Dacca in 12 to 15 days to prevent the United
Nations or any other country forcing a cease fire. !
Plan of Attack (See Map 3)
Major Effort from the East. IV Corps with three divisions plus |
a Mukti Bahini brigade to capture Chandpur, Daud Kundi,
Bhairab Bazaar with a view to capturing Dacca in the shortest
possible time.
Two Secondary Efforts one from the West and one from North
using two divisions each in the Jessore and Bogra sectors
respectively. .
One diversionary attack One brigade from the direction of
Mymensingh southwards.
General Aurora accepted that he initiated the attack against
East Pakistan soon after the monsoon period was over and much

then to move into Pakistan territory in hot pursuit. One such
incident which drew international attention was the Bogra
engagement of 21 November between Indian and Pakistani forces,
"The political directive, which tacitly accepted probing attacks
across the border, laid down that no Indian soldiers should
become prisoners during their forays into Pakistani territory, as in
that case surprise would have been lost and an international
pressure would be built up to prevent India from launching a full
scale offensive", acknowledged the army commander. Actually that
would have provided evidence of a military involvement by India
as early as October.
Indian forces entered East Pakistani territory with full force
alongwith the Mukti Bahini on the night of 20/21 November. The
attacks were no longer limited to border raids or provision of
artillery support to the rebels. Proper brigade size operations were
now launched against the Pakistani border posts. The Mukti
Bahini were directed to by-pass the defences and establish
blocking positions in the rear to cut off all routes of withdrawal. In
ordinary circumstances it would not have been easy for the enemy
to infiltrate forces deep into the rear and continue operating from
there. Paramilitary forces and local citizens could deal with such
isolated intruders but in the case of East Pakistan, by the year
1971, the Mukti Bahini were getting the support not only of
Indian troops but even of the local population.
Military situation in November
When the main Indian attack against East Pakistan began the
military situation was most unfavourable to the defenders. The
political mission of not allowing Mukti Bahini to establish a
| Bangladesh government on East Pakistan territory remained
| valid. All the troops were strung along the border in penny
packets. Most of them were deployed in the internal security role
which forced dispersement as against concentration to meet 4
major attack. The officers and men had been carrying out counter-
insurgency operations without relief for the last eight months and
were by now getting tired of continually fighting. There were
serious imbalances in the newly arrived and newly raised adhoc
formations. Some were only about two thirds of their strength.
The divisions were without their standard component of artillery
regiments. Not only were medium guns not sent to East Pakistan,

full fledged Indian attack, was wrongly conceived one can derive

was asked to pick up a few pieces from the ashes of the military
debacle the most significant amongst them would be the actions of
205 Infantry Brigade, part of 16 Infantry Division, which was
responsible for the defence of the Hilli - Bogra section in the
north-west sector of East Pakistan.

The area around Hilli was plain and dry in the month of
November. No major water obstacles existed to break the
momentum of the attack. Everything seemed tailor made for the
attackers, but yet the brigade defending Hilli withstood the
onslaught till the very end.
205 Brigade was commanded by Brigadier Tajammul Hussein
Malik who had earned his spurs at Batapur, (West Pakistan), as
the commanding officer of 3 Baloch, in September 1965, when he,
alongwith others, had stopped the advance of the Indian army
towards Lahore. This time his task was to prevent them from
reaching Bogra.
Tajammul was a product of Chakwal in the martial belt of
undivided India. He was commissioned in the 7th Rajput
Regiment in February 1947. He was known in the army for his
doggedness and his determination to pursue a course of action,
which he perceived to be correct, to the limit, irrespective of its
consequences. A streak of religious fanaticism made him
unmindful of his personal safety. It also gave him perseverance in
adversity. It was this trait in his character which made him insist
eo every inch of the area assigned to him would be defended and
at there would be no withdrawal to the designated fortress of
Bogra. (a correct attitude at the company and battalion level but
not necessarily so when fighting a corps or theatre battle).

Bahaduria.'Alongwith the depth company of 4 FF a fairly strong

the defences at Bahaduria a screen of two platoons was deployed
ahead of it to delay the enemy’s advance. They did so for one
complete day which is more than is expected from a screen
position.
It took the Indians another two days to Stage an attack against
Bahaduria. At about 4 p.m on 8 December the enemy started
shelling the area. When the artillery fire lifted an enemy
armoured regiment was seen moving forwards. Sepoys Faiz and
Yaqub who were in the forward platoon were crushed under the
tank tracks. Subedar Maskin Shah got out of his trench and
engaged a tank with his 75 millimetre recoilless rifle. He died
seconds later hit by another enemy tank. Subedar Sher Afzal, on
the orders of Major Sabir Kamal, loaded another recoilless rifle
and took a pot shot at an enemy tank 500 yards away. But no
sooner had he exposed himself, a couple of Indian tanks fired
simultaneously at Subedar Sher Afzal killing him instantly. Major
_ Sabir Kamal who was the moving spirit behind these two actions
also gave the Supreme sacrifice demanded of a soldier. No greater
honour can be given to these brave men of the Pakistan army
than the words of their bitterest enemy. Lieutenant General Jagjit
Singh Aurora, Commander Eastern Command, confessed that one
of the bloodiest battles in East Pakistan was fought at Bahaduria
Where according to him 17 Kumaon suffered 55 dead and 27
Wounded!7,

fortress which was to be defended at all costs was the town of
Jessore - the most important town after Dacca. Khulna, the only
port in his area lay south of Jessore. The divisional 2a ae

Indian II Corps, under Lieutenant General T.N. (tuby) Raina,
was deployed against 9 Infantry Division with its headquarters at
: Krishannagar, 15 miles from the East Pakistan border. The Corps
was poised for an attack on Kushtia, Jessore and Khulna and had
been given the task to prevent 9 Division from falling back to
Dacca. The Corps consisted of two infantry divisions, 4 Mountain
Division (Major General Mohinder Singh Barar) and 9 Mountain
Division (Major General Dalbir Singh). Each division had a
regiment of PT 76s (amphibious tanks) under command.
Battle of Jessore
The Jessore sector in the south-west corner of East Pakistan
extended from a line joining the towns of Jibannagar,
Kotchandpur and Kaliganj in the north to the dense forests of the
Sunderbans on the shores of the Bay of Bengal in the south. A
frontage of nearly 112 kilometres. To the east flowed the mighty
Ganges. Just across the western border with India lay the
metropolis of Calcutta - a city of teaming millions most of whose
inhabitants slept in the open. A credible threat in that direction
would have caused considerable panic amongst its civilian
population. General Dalbir Singh, confided to Brigadier
Muhammad Hayat, after the war, that if the Pakistani troops had
even advanced three kilometres towards Calcutta the people
would have fled the city.

Hayat had spent most of his career in command of troops and
handling of a brigade in operations would not normally have been

‘He had been given contradictory tasks by his superiors. While

at all costs, he was directed to "keep the enemy as far away as
possible by occupying all border observation posts (BOPs) and not
to permit any infiltration".
There were three main approaches leading to Jessore (1)
Jibannagar - Mehspur - Chuagacha - Jessore in the north, (2)
Benapol - Jingergacha - Jessore in the centre and (3) Satkhira -
Karole - Jessore in the south.
Although Eastern Command had appreciated that the major
effort of the Indian army would be against East Pakistan’s eastern
border as that was the shortest route to Dacca, it was also
apprehensive of the enemy’s thrust towards the important town of
| Jessore which was dangerously close to the international
boundary, The strongest division was, therefore, assigned this
‘ctor. 107 Brigade had been given its full complement of emer 4
armour and artillery. A divisional reserve had also been created.

Although the war had officially ended on 16 December, 107
Brigade held on to Khulna till 0800 hours 17 December. Genera]
Aurora admits that the division which was sent down to Khulna
could not capture it till the cease fire because the Pakistanis had
organised a good defensive position with a bog on one side and a
river on the other. "The fighting there could have gone on for a
long time" added the Indian army commander’.
57 Brigade (Jhenida Sub-Sector)
Brigadier Manzoor Ahmad, a soft spoken Kashmiri officer,
whose mild manners and even temperament were more suited for
.a staff appointment than the command of troops in an
unfavourable environment. A former member of the directing
staff at the prestigious Command and Staff College, Quetta he had
more than adequate knowledge for organising a proper defence
position at the brigade and divisional level.
57 Brigade, however, had only two infantry battalions as
against the standard three. He was to cover a frontage of 80
kilometres, fifteen times greater than what he had been teaching.
He not only-faced an enemy threat of one division but he had also
to protect his rear areas, routes of withdrawal and vital
installations from his own people. A major deviation from the staff
college solution had to be made, more so because of the directive
of holding every inch of territory.
Manzoor put everything he had in the shop window. 29 Baloch
was on the right covering the axis to Harding/Paksy bridge the
only vital link to 16 Division across the Ganges. 18 Punjab was
deployed on the left to guard the approach to Jhenida which was
i both, his brigade headquarters and a town which had been
prepared as a fortress for prolonged defence. A company was
detached from 18 Punjab to man an outpost at Darsana right on
the border and at the inter-brigade boundary. It was covering the
shortest approach to Jhenida. 38 FF of 107 Brigade was
immediately on its left.
Manzoor’s flanks were protected by a major river in the north
and 107 Brigade in the south. Madhumati river ran from north-
west to south-east in the eastern half of his Brigade area. The
terrain was not unduly cut up and had a reasonably good
infrastructure of a road and rail network.

Indian troops alongwith Mukties had crossed over ie se
territory and were now entrenched east of the river athabanga.
The company was ordered to clear the Mukties from own
territory. To accomplish the task 12 rounds of 3.7 artillery were
allotted. This was probably to scare the Mukties and obviate the
need for a company attack. On 9 November the company moved
‘nto a forward concentration area by midnight. At 0530 hours D
Company debouched from its forming Up place with two platoons
up. On reaching approximately 300 yards from the objective the
troops suddenly came under intense artillery, mortar and machine
gun fire. The right forward platoon led by Lieutenant G.M. Sipra,
had suffered heavily. His platoon junior commissioned officer
Naib/Subedar Akram was seriously wounded. The gallant
company commander decided to forge ahead. By now one third of
the company’s strength had been depleted, but the battalion war
cry “Nara-i-Haidri” gave them the extra courage. They assaulted
the enemy bunkers, regardless of their exposure to enemy fire.
Approximately 22 men reached the objective forcing the enemy
to take to their heels. Naik Yaqub was seen madly charging on the
enemy with his right hand raised over his head. Lance Naik
Mehdi fell at 10 yards distance from an enemy bunker with 5
bullets in his skull through his steel helmet, Lance Naik Sher
Muhammad (driver) sat on top of one of the enemy machine gun
bunkers and ordered the inmates to surrender one by one.
Subedar Ayub faked loud messages and foiled the enemy counter
attack, by indicating the pressure of a complete battalion in the
area. A Company of 29 Baloch after having crossed the river also
appeared at 0800 hours at the rear of the fleeing enemy and
inflicted heavy losses to them.
In this operation six prisoners from 1 Nagaland Battalion
(regulars) were captured for the first time in East Pakistan. It was
then learnt that this position was held by two Companies of 1
Nagaland Battalion. The position was prepared and fortified over
the last 5 days. There were approximately 100 Mukties under
command of this force. From a monitored wireless message 12 the
divisional headquarters it was learnt that the enemy had lost two
officers in this operation. D Company had also suffered heavy
losses but the enemy was routed. Captain Imtiaz and seven other
ranks were recommended for gallantry.

Lieutenant General Sagat Singh commanding IV Corps, on the

In addition to this formidable array of men and weaponry
Sagat Singh had the advantage of a Trojan House which would
subvert the fortress from within and open its doors from inside for
his troops to rush in.

36 (Adhoc) Division was a hoax. It was a misnomer. A patch-

asked to raise and take over the command of 36 (Adhoc) Division.
A tall, handsome, well built Punjabi, Stalwart from the martial
belt of Jhelum. Soldering was his families occupation for decades
but physique and family background are not the only criteria for
success in the battlefield. He only had one brigade and that too of
two battalions. A two-star general was commanding a couple of
infantry units and that’s all. His artillery support no more than a
bow and arrow. Twelve 120 mm mortars is all that he got.
His area of responsibility stretched from the northern borders
of East Pakistan between the Jamuna and the Surma rivers to its

not given any importance as the enemy threat in this area was
listed as a beefed up brigade. However, there was no major water
obstacle in between the commander of the Indian L of C troops
and his vital objective.

Evacuation
On 15 December Niazi had sent a signal to Manekshaw
accepting a conditional cease fire in East Pakistan. Major Liagat
Asrar Bukhari, commanding 4 Army Aviation Squadron in Rag
Pakistan told the General on that day that he was prepared to fly
out his team in the hours of darkness to Burma if permitted to do
so. Air Commodore Inamul Haq felt that in view of total air
superiority enjoyed by the IAF that would not be possible. Rear
Admiral Sharif opined that Liaqat should be allowed to give it 4
try as several helicopters would be prevented from falling into
enemy hands. General Niazi agreed and ordered Liagqat to take
Major General Rahim with him as he was wounded and that he
had to send some important documents through him to
Islamabad. He also informed Liagat that some nurses would also
be sent with him.
Liagat worked out his time and space and decided to fly out
from Dacca at 3 am on 16 December so that he could be across the
border and in Burmese territory before dawn. There were in all
eight helicopters. Four Mi8s (medium size helicopters) and four
Aluettes (four seaters). Liagat waited for the nurses till 3 a.m. but
was forced to leave without them as taking off after three O'clock
would have meant flying in the day-time over Bangladesh
territory which he had to avoid. Liagat flew very low to avoid
being detected. Throughout the flight no lights were switched and
no communications with any one was carried out.

426 Tragedy of Errors
When Niazi was told by the Chief of the General Staff Major
General Gul Hasan on 12 December that the Yellows are coming
from the north and the Whites from the south, he got emboldeneg
and announced his famous last words "tanks over my chest", [p
actual fact it was the Browns (Indians ) which were coming from
all directions. General Gul Hasan had passed this fake message in
Pushto to the operator in Dacca as, according to him, he was told
of this by the Chief of Staff, General Abdul Hamid.
Niazi put up a brave face based on false bravado when he sent
a signal to GHQ on 13 December. He tried to assure them that the
Dacca fortress was well organised and that he was determined to
fight it out (G 1282 dated 131500). He followed that with another
signal eight hours later (G1286 dated 132300) informing them
that he was moving to the built up area for the final battle.
Both GHQ and Eastern Command were playing a game of
bluff at that stage. Neither of them were willing to tell the other
that they had gambled and lost.
On 13 December government house Dacca was strafed by the
Indian air force. Several other targets in Dacca were being
bombed. The Indians had stepped up their psychological warfare
by spreading false rumours using Pakistan army wireless
channels. Dr Malik had come to the conclusion that East Pakistan
would soon become Bangladesh and his own life and that of his
family would not be safe if he stayed in the government house and
so on the very next day he decided to resign and move to the inter
continental hotel which by then had become a neutral zone.
General Yahya finally accepted the defeat of his army in East
| Pakistan and directed the governor and commander Eastern
| Command, in his unclassified signal of 14 December that they
should now take all necessary measures to stop the fighting and
preserve the lives of all armed forces personnel and loyal elements
in Kast Pakistan. He also informed them that his government had
moved the United Nations to urge India to stop hostilities in East
Pakistan forthwith. (G 0013, DTG 141332 EF).
The signal from the President was received at Eastern
Command headquarters at 2 P. m. on 14 December. Air
Commodore Inamul Hag, Rear Admiral Muhammad Sharif and
Major General Farman, who were also present at the
Headquarters at that time, gave their respective interpretations to

Rear Admiral Muhammad Sharif, Flag Officer commanding
Fast Pakistan (FOCEP), assumed command of the naval
establishment in the eastern wing on 9 June, 1971. His
headquarters was at Dacca. His total naval strength consisted of
eight Chinese coasters, four converted gun boats and two landing
crafts (LCTs). Eventually with local assistance he managed to
increase his force to 24 converted boats and 20 coasters. With this
in hand he had to defend East Pakistan against any external or
internal threat.
FOCEP’s tasks in East Pakistan were numerous. They
included: patrolling of sea and riverine routes to meet external
and internal threats; assist the army in amphibious operations
and provide naval gunfire support when needed; move troops and
stores by sea or by river; ground defence of naval installations and
vital port facilities; keeping ports of Chittagong and Chalna
functioning; ensuring safe movement for all riverine traffic
throughout East Pakistan and advising Eastern Command and
the martial law headquarters on all matters pertaining to inland
water transport (IWT) and maritime problems. The tasks were,
quite obviously, much beyond FOCEP’s capabilities which was
pointed out to the higher naval authorities by Admiral Sharif.
Throughout the period from June to late November FOCEP
continued to patrol most of the waterways, clearing them of
limpet mines which were being laid by the Mukti Bahini frogmen.
Naval gun boats also escorted river convoys carrying troops;
ammunition and supplies. Anti-smuggling operations to prevent
weapons being smuggled from India, Hong Kong and Singapore
were also carried out. From June onwards and right upto
November the naval gun boats cargied out combined operations
with the army to clear various areas of armed rebels.
Mukti Bahini armed with rifles, automatic weapons, 2 inch
mortars, stenguns and grenade-launchers operated, from the

On December 7, fifteen nations, including Argentina, Burundi,
Cameroons, Ghana, Honduras, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Nicaragua,
Sierra Leone, Somalia, Spain, Sudan, and Tunsia presented a
resolution to the General Assembly of the United Nations.
Resolution 2793 (XXVI) called on the governments of India and
Pakistan to take measures forthwith for an immediate ceasefire
and withdrawal of the forces to their own side of the border. It
urged both countries to intensify efforts for the voluntary return
of the East Pakistan refugees and for rendering assistance to
them’.
Mr. Yakob Malik, speaking during the debate at the General
Assembly on the recently introduced resolution, repeated the
earlier stand of his government and insisted that a ceasefire must
be accompanied immediately by recognising the will of the East
Pakistani population. Huang Hua condemned India’s aggression
and the shameless support given to it by the Soviet imperialists.
Mr. Bush, while accepting that the crisis began as a result of the
use of force by Pakistan in March, emphasised that India has the
major responsibility for broadening the crisis.
Mr. Crowe representing the United Kingdom was non-
committal. He felt that bilateral consultations inside and outside
the Security Council could halt the conflict and help in finding a
peaceful solution to the desperately complicated situation which
gave rise to the outbreak of the war. Mr. Morizet of France
believed that the only realistic measure was to obtain a cessation
of hostilities without prejudice to what may be decided
subsequently.
- _ Mr. Samer Sen speaking on behalf of India harped on the
theme of genocide and that India was forced to act in self defence.
He could now say, with some confidence, that the existence of

er had grave weaknesses but it was preferable to the
see one. He went on to say that the political problem of East
n was not that of self determination but of autonomy.

i abstentions. Resolutions passed by the General Assembly are only
recommendations. They are not binding like those passed by the
Security Council. Even there only resolutions imposing sanctions
on a member state are binding. Others are not.

Analysis
The time to take the issue to the Security Council was on 99
November when it had become quite clear that India had violated
the integrity of Pakistan on a large scale by sending its troops deep
inside Pakistan territory. It was no longer a situation where the
Indian artillery was supporting the Mukti Bahini in carrying out
forays just across the border. The Indian regular army, whose
units had been identified, were not only occupying several salients
but were advancing menacingly towards population centres.
Independent correspondents could have verified Indian
aggression against Pakistan. The electronic media could have
vividly portrayed the fact as it existed on the ground, giving the
United States and China an opportunity to demand the
withdrawal of Indian forces from East Pakistan as early as 22
November. The Soviet Union, of-course, would have vetoed any
such resolution as they did on 5 December but it would have given
more time to friendly countries to increase the pressure on India.
Taking up the matter at the Security Council after 3 December
was not correctly timed as soon thereafter ‘resistance began to
crumble in East Pakistan. Members of the Security Council who
had been supporting Pakistan’s belated efforts to arrive at a
peaceful political settlement became lukewarm as the military
situation in East Pakistan began to turn in India’s favour.
Pakistan also lost an Opportunity to extricate its troops from
East Pakistan honourably when it did not accept the Russian
resolution of 5 December. The Soviet resolution, as mentioned
earlier, called for a political settlement and an end to all acts of
Violence by the Pakistan armed forces in East Pakistan. A
ceasefire in situ could perhaps have been worked out as the Soviet
Union was the only country at that stage which could have
stopped India continuing its advance into East Pakistan. Of
course, the only political solution acceptable to India and the
Awami League would have been total independence. There was 0
way that could be stopped. It could have been achieved, however;
without the humiliation of having 93,000 prisoners in Indian
camps for three years.

There was a clear cut division between the civilian
management of war and the military plans to accomplish the
national objective. Although no Joint Staff Headquarters existeg

ministry of defence to prepare for and handle the higher direction
of war. Lower down, command headquarters had tactical air

In Pakistan, the President sat in the Military Operations room
at GHQ to get reports of a battle raging a thousand miles away
over which he had no control. There was also intermittent breaks
between Eastern Command and CMLA HQ as occasionally the
President, his Chief of Staff and the Principal Staff Officer were

general staff were reportedly not on talking terms. Neither was
the CGS getting along with other PSOs at GHQ. For such a
situation to exist at the highest military headquarters when the
country’s integrity was at state, is unpardonable.
Complete control over the forces one commands is a sina qua
non for success on the battlefield. It is equally important in a
theatre of operations.

battle had been lost from Day 1. With units split into companies

By the time the real fighting started in November the troops
had been engaged in fighting an elusive enemy for over eight
months. They had by then become tired and exhausted. Their
morale was further adversely affected when they began to realise
that the local population had turned against them. Every day that
; passed brought no relief or reinforcements. A feeling of isolation
and strategic encirclement began to creep in when contact with
other units and formations began to be lost due to the activities of
the guerrillas. "General Niazi had lost the will to fight on
December 7"!6 noted Justice Hamood-ur-Rahman.
An army, hated and despised by its own people, cannot be
expected to retain its morale nor its discipline for long. That was
the situation into which the army had been placed because of the
follies of its leadership in 1971. Indian propaganda and the
international electronic and print media carried exaggerated
;stories of the success by the Mukti Bahini as part of an
orchestrated psychological campaign against the troops in East
Pakistan, which also had an impact on the fighting spirit of the
soldiers.
Lack of air support
In modern warfare air power plays almost a decisive role. The
side that can achieve even local air superiority can cause so great a
damage to ground forces, logistic installations and command
headquarters that further military operations become untenable.
The air situation in East Pakistan was even worse. Just three days
after the western front was opened the Indian air force succeeded
in making the lone PAF squadron in-effective. The only airfield
available was made non-operational and when the remaining PAF
: pilots were flown out during the war the skies over East Pakistan
were totally dominated by the IAF. It fully exploited the third
dimension of warfare, which hastened the fall of Dacca.
Naval Blockade
With the banning of overflights over Indian territory by Mrs.
Gandhi after the ‘Ganga’ incident at <a only way to re
supply East Pakistan was by a circuitous route via Sri Lanka by |
sea. As the D Day drew near the Indian navy imposed 4 naval |
blockade of East Pakistan thus cutting off the only remaining link —
with the eastern wing. |

Awami League’s Six-Points Formula
As announced in the Awami League election manifesto the Six Points were:
1. The character of the Government should be federal and parliamentary, jn
which elections to the Federal Legislature and to the Legislatures of the
federating units would be direct and on the basis of universal adult franchise.
Representation in the Federal Legislature would be on the basis of
population. |
2. The Federal Government would be responsible only for defence and foreign
affairs and, subject to the conditions provided in (3) below, currency.
3. There would be two separate currencies mutually or freely convertible in each
wing for each region, or in the alternative a single currency, subject to the
establishment of a federal reserve system in which there would be regional
federal reserve banks which would devise measures to prevent the transfer of
resources and flight of capital from one region to another.
4. Fiscal policy would be the responsibility of the federating units. The Federal
Government would be provided with the requisite revenue resources for
meeting the requirements of defence and foreign affairs, which revenue
resources would be automatically appropriable by the Federal Government in
the manner provided and on the basis of the ratio to be determined by the
procedure laid down in the Constitution. Such constitutional provisions
would ensure that the Federal Government’s revenue requirements were met
consistently with the objective of ensuring control over the fiscal policy by the
Governments of the federating units.
5. Constitutional provisions would be made to enable separate accounts to be
maintained of the foreign exchange earnings of each of the federating units.
The foreign exchange requirements of the Federal Government would be met
by the Governments of the federating units on the basis of a ratio to be
determined in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Constitution.
The regional Governments would have powers under the Constitution to
negotiate foreign trade and aid within the framework of the foreign policy of
the country, which would be the responsibility of the Federal Government.
6. The Government of the federating units would be empowered to maintain &
militia or paramilitary force in order to contribute effectively towards
national security.

For President of Pakistan (.) your G-0001 of 092300 Dec (.) As the
responsibility of taking the final and fateful decision has been given to me I
am handing over the following note to Assistance Secretary General Mr. Paul
Mark Henry after your approval. Note begins (.) It was never the intention of
the Armed Forces of Pakistan to involve themselves in an all out war on the
soil of East Pakistan (.) However a situation arose which compelled the
Armed Forces to take defensive action (.) The intention of the Government of
Pakistan was always to decide the issues in East Pakistan by means of a
political solution for which negotiations were a foot (.) The armed forces have
fought heroically against heavy odds and can still continue to do so but in
order to avoid further bloodshed and loss of innocent lives I am making the
following proposals (.) As the conflict arose as a result of political causes, it
must end with a political solution (.) I therefore having been authorised by
the President of Pakistan do hereby call upon the elected representatives of
East Pakistan to arrange for the peaceful formation of the Government in
Dacea (.) In making this offer I feel duty bound to say the will of the people of
East Pakistan would demand the immediate vacation of their land by the
Indian forces as well (.) I therefore call upon the United Nations to arrange
for a peaceful transfer of power and request (.) one (.) an immediate ceasefire
(.) two (.) Repatriation with honour of the Armed Forces of Pakistan to West
Pakistan (.) three (.) repatriation of all West Pakistan personnel desirous of
returning to West Pakistan (.) four (.) The safety of all persons settled in East
Pakistan since 1947 (.) five (.) Guarantee of no reprisals against any person in

definite proposal for peaceful transfer of power (.) The question of surrender
of Armed Forces would not be considered and does not arise and if this
