PREFACE AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
Pakistan had been described by many western and Indian
writers as a geographical nonsensity and a country disfigured at
birth. Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, the well known Muslim
nationalist leader and the president of the All India Congress,
predicted that Pakistan, in its present shape, would not last more
than a-quarter of a century. His prediction came true. But not
because of the unique shape of the country, not even because of
the differences in language and culture of the two wings but
because of the follies of its people and because of the selfishness,
insincerity and short sightedness of its leaders. The most
important of all because of the ignominious role played by India 1
during the East Pakistan Crisis,
Come December each year, the nation is reminded of the
break-up of the country and the humiliation suffered by its armed
forces at the hands of its bitterest adversary. Unfortunately none
of the actors, dead or alive, who strutted about on the stage during
those crucial days, accepted that they faltered in advocating or
implementing the policies which led to the tragedy of the
disintegration of Pakistan.
The political leaders blame the army junta. The army generals '
blame the politicians, Independent political analysts blame both.
Indian writers harp on the tune of the exploitation of East Bengal
by the West Pakistani leadership. Pakistani authors highlight the
statements of a large number of influential Indians, including
Indira Gandhi, that the dismemberment of Pakistan would be in
India’s national interest and that India should not miss the
‘opportunity of a life time’ provided to them in 1971.
It is an irony of fate that the very people who were in the
)) Vanguard of the Pakistan movement, whose area was the only
Muslim majority province of undivided India which had a Muslim
League ministry and whose illustrious son had not only moved
but, allegedly, drafted the Lahore Resolution, fought a bitter
Struggle, thirty years later, to destroy a country which -they
themselves had helped to build.

16 :
How did this happen? what were the causes of the alienation of
the Bengalis from their co-citizens in the western wing? Why was
it not possible to stop the widening gap between the two halves of
Pakistan? Was the separate homeland for the Muslims of the
subcontinent merely a stepping stone for the Bengali politicians,
towards an independent Bangladesh? Could the armed forces have
avoided a humiliating surrender? These and many other related
' questions came to my mind during my research into the causes of
the tragic outcome.
This is the result of nearly three years of hard labour. It is
based on a deep study of documents, newspapers, articles, books
and personal interviews of those who were then at the helm of
affairs. The book focuses on the geo-strategic implication of a
country divided by a thousand miles of enemy territory. It brings
out the causes of the progressive alienation of the Bengalis from
West Pakistan. It highlights the political bitnglings of the civil and
military leadership during the first twenty-four years of Pakistan’s
existence. It analyses the war plans of India and Pakistan in 1971.
It focuses attention on the yole of India in this sordid drama and
finally it looks into the impact of the dismemberment of Pakistan
on India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. :
I have tried to disprove a few generalizations. The important
ones being that the dismantlement was a foregone conclusion
, because the only thing that was common between East and West
Pakistan was religion and the only link the PIA. The second ,
theory is the oft repeated accusation of the exploitation of East
Bengal by West Pakistan. I have tried to prove by facts and figures
that it is not entirely true. The third fallacy which does not stand
scrutiny is a fact often quoted by Indian academicians that there
was a deliberate attempt by the Punjabi hierarchy to keep the
East Pakistani’s out of the civil service and the armed forces. It is
true that the Bengalis did not have a share in the government in
~ proportion to their population but the causes lay elsewhere.

In 1974, the late Lieutenant General Agha Ibrahim Akram,
well known author of the book, Sword of Allah, told me about
writing his second book on the advent of Islam in Iran. On my
saying "why do you not write about the dismemberment of

Background
Geographical Characteristics
East Pakistan, lying at the eastern extremity of the Indian
subcontinent, differed from its western wing in its geographic
location, physical features, socio-economic conditions and in its
security environment. Separated from the rest of Pakistan by
1,600 kilometres of Indian territory it was more easily vulnerable
to internal and external pressures than the rest of the country.
Abul Kalam Azad opined that Mr. Jinnah did not seem to realize
that geography was against him!. He was not too far wrong.
With an area covering 143,998 square kilometres it was
smaller in size than almost all other provinces of Pakistan. Its
population of 40 million in 1947 was, however, greater than all the
four administrative units in the west combined. This numerical
superiority coupled with the volatile nature of an ever increasingly
frustrated community shifted the dynamics of power to the streets
of East Bengal. .
East Pakistan, except for a very small border with Burma, was
surrounded on all sides by India. In the west lay the Indian state
of West Bengal. In the north was Magalaya and Assam, in the east
Tripura and Mizogram and in the south the Indian dominated Bay
of Bengal. Geography, therefore, very much favored India if and
when it decided to use its military instrument to achieve its
political objective. Pakistan’s eastern wing could easily be cut off
from the other half, in fact from the rest of the world, by India
because of its peculiar geographic location.
The three main river systems, each broad enough to look like a
sea of water, divided the country into four isolated regions. The
western sector lay between the Bay of Bengal and the
Ganges/Padma with Khulna, Jessore and Faridpur being the
main towns. The northern portion was wedged in between the
Jamuna and the Brahmaputra/Meghna. Saidpur and Rangpur in
the north and Bogra further south were the nodal points. East
and south of the Meghna lay the tea gardens of Sylhet and the
- undulating ground around Comilla and Chittagong.

These formidable water obstacles, unbridged except in very

split the defenders into isolated pockets and gave advancing
enemy columns secure flanks. They presented no obstacle when
moving along them but were almost insurmountable to those who

The 6,000 square kilometres Deltaic region, along the coast
with its numerous creeks and water inlets, with its swamps and
thickets, was impregnable to friends and foes alike. The forests of
the Sunderbans, along the southwest coast, immortalized by the
famous English novelist, John Masters, and those of Mahdopur
near Dacca restricted movement in those areas. The Chittagong
Hill Tracts, in the east rising to heights of 2,000 feet, forested and
mountainous, was ideal for guerrilla actions.
Mention must be made of the area around Dacca, known in
military circles as the Dacca bowl or the Dacca triangle. A flat and
open country about a 100 kilometres wide and 60 kilometres deep.
It lay between three major river systems with the mighty Jamuna
and Ganges in the west, the Dareshwari river in the south and the
Meghna in the east. The only approach to Dacca which did not
need the crossing of a major river was from the north,
Communications .
Communication infrastructure was poor. Roads were narrow,
and few and far between. Most of them frequently ended on river
banks from where the loads had to be transferred on to steamers
and back again on to the single lane asphalt highway. Chittagong
and Khulna were two sea-going ports with Chandpur providing
only an inland water transport (IWT) facility. A railway line did
connect the capital to Rajshahi in the west, Saidpur in the north,
Sylhet in the north-east and the port of Chittagong in the south,
but not without the restriction of unloading and loading on to
ferries as construction of railway bridges across the rivers was
only possible in one or two places. Most of the movement, both
civilian and military, was along rivers and streams by naukas
(country boats) and steamers. With cross country movement
difficult, even during the dry season, all major traffic had to be
confined to the few available metalled roads, interdiction of which
became comparatively easier during war.

Geographical Characteristics
Although the communication network in East Pakistan was
generally poor the roads and railways leading to the international /
border from Indian West Bengal were well] developed. Calcutta, “
the largest city of India and the headquarters of India’s Eastern
Command, was only 100 kilometres away from the Pakistani town
of Jessore. It was connected to it by several metalled roads and
broadguage railway tracks. Assembly of forces on the Indian side
was easier.
Vulnerable Salients .
The geographical configuration of East Pakistan created a
number of salients and narrow necks of land which, while making
them vulnerable to attacks, also provided opportunities to disrupt
India’s vital lines of communication. Patchagarh salient in the
north-west jutted into the Siliguri gap connecting West Bengal
with Assam. Even a small thrust northwards could create
difficulties for India’s Eastern Command. Though 40 kilometres
long it had a width of only 10 kilometres. A major road from
Jalpaiguri (India) to Tatulia ran through it. Kurigram salient a
little further east had only a width of 6 kilometres. Belonia east of
Comilla was surrounded on three sides by India and posed a
serious problem for the defenders. The most vulnerable neck of
land in East Pakistan was Feni which was only a stone’s throw
away from India. An advance of only a few kilometres ‘could severe
Chittagong port and a large tract of East Pakistan, without any
major effort, from the rest of the province.
Climate
East Bengal, lying astride the tropic of cancer, had a hot and
humid climate. Temperatures in summer rose up to 33 C°
(91 °F). Not very hot from South Asian standards but what made
the living uncomfortable was the humidity. Bengal catches the full
blast of the south-west monsoons. With an average rainfall of over
2,500 millimeters (100 inches), concentrated during the period
between April and September, major military operations could
take place during the winter months only.

_ Historical Perspective
Bengal was conquered by the Mughals in 1202 AD by
Muhammad Bakhtyar Khilji, a subordinate commander of Sultan ,
Qutubuddin Aiybak‘*. It was the first province of the Mughal (
Empire to pass fully into the hands of the British. Since the
British had snatched power from the Muslims they were
apprehensive of any attempt by them to try and regain their lost
kingdom. They, therefore, made a concerted plan to suppress the
‘Muslims and encourage the Hindus in their newly acquired
domain of Bengal.
Partition of Bengal and its Annulment
The dominance of the Hindu landlord, businessmen and
traders increased to such an extent in Bengal that the Muslims
demanded the partition of the province so that they could free
themselves from the Hindu Bhadrulok (landlord). Bengal was
partitioned in 1905. and the districts of Dacca, Rajshahi and
Chittagong (later to become part of Pakistan) were separated from
Western Bengal. "The Hindus considered the partition of Bengal
as an attempt to create a Muslim state in Eastern Bengal"®. Most
of the Hindus, resented the breakaway and forced Lord Curzon,
the then viceroy of India, to annul the partition of Bengal. The two
frontiers were united again by a proclamation made by King
George V at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.
Even after the annulment of the partition of Bengal the
’ Muslims continued to work towards creating better opportunities
for themselves. To compete with the Hindus in the field of
education, the Muslims of Bengal demanded the establishment of

Causes of Alienation
The most significant effect of the geographical separation of the
two wings of Pakistan was the alienation of East Bengal from the
rest of the country. Many were the reasons put forward by the
_ Bengalis for_the bitterness they felt towards their co-citizens in
the west. Some were, of course, exaggerated to achieve the
objective of selfish individuals. A few were completely false and
part of a disinformation campaign. But none of the issues were so
great, in the beginning, to be unsurmountable.
What was needed was a clearer understanding of the unique ;
nature of Pakistan’s geography and its peculiar demographic ~~
characteristics. A sincere effort was also required, not only to
devise, but to implement, policies which could have removed the ~
suspicion and mistrust which had crept into the minds of the
people on both sides. The politicians, military leadership, \
bureaucrats and businessmen all shared this responsibility. «
Tragically they failed to deliver. Mistakes were made soon after
independence. Regional _ political leadeys and frustrated
intellectuals capitalised on them. Errors kept multiplying;
emotions kept rising; demands and their suppression kept
growing till it was too late to prevent the dismemberment of the
country aided and abetted by a hostile neighbour.
/
What were the main causes for the glienation? These could be
grouped under cultural, economic, political and military. Behind

Every one gets back to business as usual The defeated politician

East Bengal Regiments (EBR)
The first and second battalions of the East Bengal Regiment
were raised in Kurmitola (Dacca) in 1948 when General Ayub
Khan was the GOC in East Bengal. Their class composition was
100 percent Bengali. General Ayub did not raise any objection to
this change in the composition of the East Bengal Regiment units.
perhaps due to the fact that initially it was presumed that they
would only serve in the eastern wing. The question of a whole unit
revolting could never have crossed his mind a year after the
creation of Pakistan. A five percent quota for recruitment of
Bengali personnel had, however, been placed which later was
removed and so by 1965/66 five battalions of the East Bengal
Regiment were on the ground.

Jessore. Each sector was composed of six wings of 450 men each.
Most of the men were Bengalis while their officers came both

Strategic Orientation
The geographical separation of the two wings of Pakistan made
it virtually impossible to plan for a co-ordinated defence of the
whole of the country. The options available were either to raise
two self-contained independent armed forces, each capable of
defending its own area of responsibility against a numerically
superior enemy, or to provide for a minimum force in a less
vulnerable region with the major defensive strength lying in the
other. |
In the case of the former, the Indians would have been
compelled to pay a heavy price to achieve their objective of
dismembering Pakistan. Economically, however, such an option
could not have been sustained and the danger of the country
crumbling from within due to its people being deprived of the
basic necessities would have been very much there.
In the latter case one or the other wing would remain
dangerously exposed. Working on interior lines the Indians had
the ability of concentrating their armed forces against one flank at
Pane while denying that facility to Pakistan. Both the wings of
akistan had their strengths and weaknesses.

Rear Admiral Muhammad Sharif, Flag Officer commanding
Fast Pakistan (FOCEP), assumed command of the naval
establishment in the eastern wing on 9 June, 1971. His
headquarters was at Dacca. His total naval strength consisted of
eight Chinese coasters, four converted gun boats and two landing
crafts (LCTs). Eventually with local assistance he managed to
increase his force to 24 converted boats and 20 coasters. With this
in hand he had to defend East Pakistan against any external or
internal threat.
FOCEP’s tasks in East Pakistan were numerous. They
included: patrolling of sea and riverine routes to meet external
and internal threats; assist the army in amphibious operations
and provide naval gunfire support when needed; move troops and
stores by sea or by river; ground defence of naval installations and
vital port facilities; keeping ports of Chittagong and Chalna
functioning; ensuring safe movement for all riverine traffic
throughout East Pakistan and advising Eastern Command and
the martial law headquarters on all matters pertaining to inland
water transport (IWT) and maritime problems. The tasks were,
quite obviously, much beyond FOCEP’s capabilities which was
pointed out to the higher naval authorities by Admiral Sharif.
Throughout the period from June to late November FOCEP
continued to patrol most of the waterways, clearing them of
limpet mines which were being laid by the Mukti Bahini frogmen.
Naval gun boats also escorted river convoys carrying troops;
ammunition and supplies. Anti-smuggling operations to prevent
weapons being smuggled from India, Hong Kong and Singapore
were also carried out. From June onwards and right upto
November the naval gun boats cargied out combined operations
with the army to clear various areas of armed rebels.
Mukti Bahini armed with rifles, automatic weapons, 2 inch
mortars, stenguns and grenade-launchers operated, from the

Analysis
The time to take the issue to the Security Council was on 99
November when it had become quite clear that India had violated
the integrity of Pakistan on a large scale by sending its troops deep
inside Pakistan territory. It was no longer a situation where the
Indian artillery was supporting the Mukti Bahini in carrying out
forays just across the border. The Indian regular army, whose
units had been identified, were not only occupying several salients
but were advancing menacingly towards population centres.
Independent correspondents could have verified Indian
aggression against Pakistan. The electronic media could have
vividly portrayed the fact as it existed on the ground, giving the
United States and China an opportunity to demand the
withdrawal of Indian forces from East Pakistan as early as 22
November. The Soviet Union, of-course, would have vetoed any
such resolution as they did on 5 December but it would have given
more time to friendly countries to increase the pressure on India.
Taking up the matter at the Security Council after 3 December
was not correctly timed as soon thereafter ‘resistance began to
crumble in East Pakistan. Members of the Security Council who
had been supporting Pakistan’s belated efforts to arrive at a
peaceful political settlement became lukewarm as the military
situation in East Pakistan began to turn in India’s favour.
Pakistan also lost an Opportunity to extricate its troops from
East Pakistan honourably when it did not accept the Russian
resolution of 5 December. The Soviet resolution, as mentioned
earlier, called for a political settlement and an end to all acts of
Violence by the Pakistan armed forces in East Pakistan. A
ceasefire in situ could perhaps have been worked out as the Soviet
Union was the only country at that stage which could have
stopped India continuing its advance into East Pakistan. Of
course, the only political solution acceptable to India and the
Awami League would have been total independence. There was 0
way that could be stopped. It could have been achieved, however;

camps for three years.

Awami League’s Six-Points Formula
As announced in the Awami League election manifesto the Six Points were:
1. The character of the Government should be federal and parliamentary, jn
which elections to the Federal Legislature and to the Legislatures of the
federating units would be direct and on the basis of universal adult franchise.
Representation in the Federal Legislature would be on the basis of
population. |
2. The Federal Government would be responsible only for defence and foreign
affairs and, subject to the conditions provided in (3) below, currency.
3. There would be two separate currencies mutually or freely convertible in each
wing for each region, or in the alternative a single currency, subject to the
establishment of a federal reserve system in which there would be regional
federal reserve banks which would devise measures to prevent the transfer of
resources and flight of capital from one region to another.
4. Fiscal policy would be the responsibility of the federating units. The Federal
Government would be provided with the requisite revenue resources for
meeting the requirements of defence and foreign affairs, which revenue
resources would be automatically appropriable by the Federal Government in
the manner provided and on the basis of the ratio to be determined by the
procedure laid down in the Constitution. Such constitutional provisions
would ensure that the Federal Government’s revenue requirements were met
consistently with the objective of ensuring control over the fiscal policy by the
Governments of the federating units.
5. Constitutional provisions would be made to enable separate accounts to be
maintained of the foreign exchange earnings of each of the federating units.
The foreign exchange requirements of the Federal Government would be met
by the Governments of the federating units on the basis of a ratio to be
determined in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Constitution.
The regional Governments would have powers under the Constitution to
negotiate foreign trade and aid within the framework of the foreign policy of
the country, which would be the responsibility of the Federal Government.
6. The Government of the federating units would be empowered to maintain &
militia or paramilitary force in order to contribute effectively towards
national security.

PREFACE AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
Pakistan had been described by many western and Indian
writers as a geographical nonsensity and a country disfigured at
birth.

Maulana Abul Kalam Azad, the well known Muslim
nationalist leader and the president of the All India Congress,
predicted that Pakistan, in its present shape, would not last more
than a-quarter of a century.
His prediction came true.

But not
because of the unique shape of the country, not even because of
the differences in language and culture of the two wings but
because of the follies of its people and because of the selfishness,
insincerity and short sightedness of its leaders.

The most
important of all because of the ignominious role played by India 1
during the East Pakistan Crisis,
Come December each year, the nation is reminded of the

Background
Geographical Characteristics
East Pakistan, lying at the eastern extremity of the Indian
subcontinent, differed from its western wing in its geographic
location, physical features, socio-economic conditions and in its
security environment.

Separated from the rest of Pakistan by
1,600 kilometres of Indian territory it was more easily vulnerable
to internal and external pressures than the rest of the country.
Abul Kalam Azad opined that Mr.

Jinnah did not seem to realize
that geography was against him!.
He was not too far wrong.

With an area covering 143,998 square kilometres it was
smaller in size than almost all other provinces of Pakistan.

Its
population of 40 million in 1947 was, however, greater than all the
four administrative units in the west combined.

This numerical
superiority coupled with the volatile nature of an ever increasingly
frustrated community shifted the dynamics of power to the streets
of East Bengal. .

East Pakistan, except for a very small border with Burma, was
surrounded on all sides by India.

In the west lay the Indian state
of West Bengal.

In the north was Magalaya and Assam, in the east
Tripura and Mizogram and in the south the Indian dominated Bay
of Bengal.

Geography, therefore, very much favored India if and
when it decided to use its military instrument to achieve its
political objective.

Pakistan’s eastern wing could easily be cut off
from the other half, in fact from the rest of the world, by India
because of its peculiar geographic location.

The three main river systems, each broad enough to look like a
sea of water, divided the country into four isolated regions.

The
western sector lay between the Bay of Bengal and the
Ganges/Padma with Khulna, Jessore and Faridpur being the
main towns.

The northern portion was wedged in between the
Jamuna and the Brahmaputra/Meghna.

Saidpur and Rangpur in
the north and Bogra further south were the nodal points.

East
and south of the Meghna lay the tea gardens of Sylhet and the
- undulating ground around Comilla and Chittagong.

A flat and
open country about a 100 kilometres wide and 60 kilometres deep.

It lay between three major river systems with the mighty Jamuna

Meghna in the east.

The only approach to Dacca which did not
need the crossing of a major river was from the north,
Communications .
Communication infrastructure was poor.

Roads were narrow,
and few and far between.

Most of them frequently ended on river
banks from where the loads had to be transferred on to steamers
and back again on to the single lane asphalt highway.

Chittagong
and Khulna were two sea-going ports with Chandpur providing
only an inland water transport (IWT) facility.

A railway line did
connect the capital to Rajshahi in the west, Saidpur in the north,
Sylhet in the north-east and the port of Chittagong in the south,
but not without the restriction of unloading and loading on to
ferries as construction of railway bridges across the rivers was
only possible in one or two places.

Most of the movement, both
civilian and military, was along rivers and streams by naukas
(country boats) and steamers.

With cross country movement
difficult, even during the dry season, all major traffic had to be
confined to the few available metalled roads, interdiction of which
became comparatively easier during war.

Geographical Characteristics
Although the communication network in East Pakistan was
generally poor the roads and railways leading to the international /
border from Indian West Bengal were well] developed.

Calcutta, “
the largest city of India and the headquarters of India’s Eastern
Command, was only 100 kilometres away from the Pakistani town
of Jessore.

It was connected to it by several metalled roads and
broadguage railway tracks.

Assembly of forces on the Indian side
was easier.
Vulnerable Salients .

The geographical configuration of East Pakistan created a
number of salients and narrow necks of land which, while making
them vulnerable to attacks, also provided opportunities to disrupt
India’s vital lines of communication.

Patchagarh salient in the
north-west jutted into the Siliguri gap connecting West Bengal
with Assam.

Even a small thrust northwards could create
difficulties for India’s Eastern Command.

Though 40 kilometres
long it had a width of only 10 kilometres.

A major road from
Jalpaiguri (India) to Tatulia ran through it.

Kurigram salient a
little further east had only a width of 6 kilometres.

Belonia east of
Comilla was surrounded on three sides by India and posed a
serious problem for the defenders.

The most vulnerable neck of
land in East Pakistan was Feni which was only a stone’s throw
away from India.

An advance of only a few kilometres ‘could severe
Chittagong port and a large tract of East Pakistan, without any
major effort, from the rest of the province.

Climate
East Bengal, lying astride the tropic of cancer, had a hot and
humid climate.

Temperatures in summer rose up to 33 C°
(91 °F).

Not very hot from South Asian standards but what made
the living uncomfortable was the humidity.

Bengal catches the full
blast of the south-west monsoons.

With an average rainfall of over
2,500 millimeters (100 inches), concentrated during the period
between April and September, major military operations could
take place during the winter months only.

Partition of Bengal and its Annulment
The dominance of the Hindu landlord, businessmen and
traders increased to such an extent in Bengal that the Muslims
demanded the partition of the province so that they could free
themselves from the Hindu Bhadrulok (landlord).

Bengal was
partitioned in 1905. and the districts of Dacca, Rajshahi and
Chittagong (later to become part of Pakistan) were separated from
Western Bengal.

"The Hindus considered the partition of Bengal
as an attempt to create a Muslim state in Eastern Bengal"®.

Most
of the Hindus, resented the breakaway and forced Lord Curzon,
the then viceroy of India, to annul the partition of Bengal.

The two
frontiers were united again by a proclamation made by King
George V at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.

Even after the annulment of the partition of Bengal the
’ Muslims continued to work towards creating better opportunities
for themselves.

education, the Muslims of Bengal demanded the establishment of

A subsidiary

the martial law headquarters on all matters pertaining to inland
water transport (IWT) and maritime problems.

The time to take the issue to the Security Council was on 99
November when it had become quite clear that India had violated
the integrity of Pakistan on a large scale by sending its troops deep
inside Pakistan territory.

It was no longer a situation where the
Indian artillery was supporting the Mukti Bahini in carrying out
forays just across the border.

The Indian regular army, whose
units had been identified, were not only occupying several salients
but were advancing menacingly towards population centres.

Independent correspondents could have verified Indian
aggression against Pakistan.

The electronic media could have
vividly portrayed the fact as it existed on the ground, giving the
United States and China an opportunity to demand the
withdrawal of Indian forces from East Pakistan as early as 22
November.

The Soviet Union, of-course, would have vetoed any
such resolution as they did on 5 December but it would have given
more time to friendly countries to increase the pressure on India.

Taking up the matter at the Security Council after 3 December
was not correctly timed as soon thereafter ‘resistance began to
crumble in East Pakistan.

Members of the Security Council who
had been supporting Pakistan’s belated efforts to arrive at a
peaceful political settlement became lukewarm as the military
situation in East Pakistan began to turn in India’s favour.

Pakistan also lost an Opportunity to extricate its troops from
East Pakistan honourably when it did not accept the Russian
resolution of 5 December.

The Soviet resolution, as mentioned
earlier, called for a political settlement and an end to all acts of
Violence by the Pakistan armed forces in East Pakistan.

A
ceasefire in situ could perhaps have been worked out as the Soviet

Awami League’s Six-Points Formula
As announced in the Awami League election manifesto the Six Points were:
1.

The character of the Government should be federal and parliamentary, jn
which elections to the Federal Legislature and to the Legislatures of the
federating units would be direct and on the basis of universal adult franchise.

Representation in the Federal Legislature would be on the basis of
population. |
2.

The Federal Government would be responsible only for defence and foreign
affairs and, subject to the conditions provided in (3) below, currency.
3.

There would be two separate currencies mutually or freely convertible in each
wing for each region, or in the alternative a single currency, subject to the
establishment of a federal reserve system in which there would be regional
federal reserve banks which would devise measures to prevent the transfer of
resources and flight of capital from one region to another.
4.
Fiscal policy would be the responsibility of the federating units.

The Federal
Government would be provided with the requisite revenue resources for
meeting the requirements of defence and foreign affairs, which revenue
resources would be automatically appropriable by the Federal Government in
the manner provided and on the basis of the ratio to be determined by the
procedure laid down in the Constitution.

Such constitutional provisions
would ensure that the Federal Government’s revenue requirements were met
consistently with the objective of ensuring control over the fiscal policy by the
Governments of the federating units.
5.

Constitutional provisions would be made to enable separate accounts to be
maintained of the foreign exchange earnings of each of the federating units.

The foreign exchange requirements of the Federal Government would be met
by the Governments of the federating units on the basis of a ratio to be
determined in accordance with the procedure laid down in the Constitution.

The regional Governments would have powers under the Constitution to
negotiate foreign trade and aid within the framework of the foreign policy of
the country, which would be the responsibility of the Federal Government.
6.

The Government of the federating units would be empowered to maintain &
militia or paramilitary force in order to contribute effectively towards
national security.
